items.title: L1: What Civil Service Jobs is
items.source: Civil Service Jobs website; GOV.UK, Working for the Civil Service
items.body: Civil Service Jobs is the official website where most vacancies in the UK Civil Service are advertised. It is run for government departments and their agencies, and it is free to use. You never pay to see a vacancy, to apply or to be considered for a job. The web address ends in .gov.uk, which shows that it is a government website. Vacancies come from many departments, such as the Department for Work and Pensions, HM Revenue and Customs and the Ministry of Justice. Each advert has a job title, a department, a grade, a location, a salary and a closing date. The grade shows the level of the job. Entry-level roles are usually Administrative Assistant (AA) or Administrative Officer (AO). Above these come Executive Officer (EO), Higher Executive Officer (HEO) and Senior Executive Officer (SEO). An Administrative Officer role is a common first step for people with no formal qualifications, because many AO adverts do not ask for a degree or A-levels. Some adverts are open to everyone. Others are open only to people who already work in the Civil Service. The advert itself says which. A few jobs are also advertised in other places, but Civil Service Jobs is the main place to look.

items.title: L1: Words you will see on an advert
items.source: Civil Service Jobs adverts; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: A Civil Service advert uses a few words that are worth learning before you apply. The job title says what the role is called, such as Administrative Officer. The department is the part of government that employs you. The grade is the level of the job. The location tells you where you would work, and some roles allow working from home for part of the week. The salary is what you are paid, and it may differ between London and other places. The closing date is the last time you can send in your application. The reference number is a code that identifies the vacancy, and it is useful to keep when you track your applications. The summary of the role describes the team and the main duties. The person specification lists what the successful applicant needs. Essential criteria are things you must be able to show, for example the right to work in the UK. Desirable criteria are extra things that help but are not required. The word applicant means a person who applies. The word sift means the first screening of applications. The advert also names the working pattern, such as full time, part time or flexible, and it lists how you will be assessed.

items.title: L1: Your account and profile
items.body: To apply for most Civil Service jobs you first create an account on the Civil Service Jobs website. You need an email address and a password. Choose a password that is hard to guess and do not share it with anyone. Keep your email address safe too, because the website sends messages about your applications to that address. Once you have an account you fill in your profile. The profile holds your personal and contact details. You fill it in once, and each application then starts with your details already in place. This saves time and cuts down on mistakes. Check that your profile is correct before every application, especially your phone number and email address. If these are wrong, you may miss an invitation to a test or interview. Look in your junk or spam folder from time to time, because messages from the website can end up there. Never give your password to anyone who contacts you, even if they say they are from the Civil Service. The website will not ask you for your bank details to apply. If you are unsure whether a message is real, go to the website directly by typing the address yourself.

items.title: L1: Searching for jobs and setting up alerts
items.body: The Civil Service Jobs website has a search tool. You can type a word such as administrative or the name of a department, and the site lists matching vacancies. You can then narrow the results with filters. The filters include location, grade, department, working pattern and salary. For example, you could choose Administrative Officer as the grade and pick a city near your home. Fewer results appear, and they are more useful. You can then save the search. A saved search remembers the words and filters you picked, so you do not need to enter them again. You can also switch on job alerts for a saved search. An alert is an email that tells you when a new vacancy matches. This helps because adverts do not stay open for long, and some close after only a week or two. Check your alerts regularly and open any that look suitable straight away. Remember that many departments advertise similar jobs, so try more than one search, for instance a different location or a similar grade. If you see no results, widen the search by removing a filter.

items.title: L1: The main stages in order
items.source: Civil Service Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Applying for a Civil Service job follows a pattern, although the details vary between departments and roles. The first stage is the application. This may be a form, a personal statement, a CV or written answers about your behaviours. The second stage is the sift. In the sift, recruiters read the applications and compare them with the criteria in the advert. Only people who meet the standard move on. Some roles then include online tests. Typical tests look at verbal skills, numbers or situational judgement. Many entry-level roles include tests, but not all do. After that comes an interview or assessment, and this is often held by video. If you do well, the department makes a conditional offer. The word conditional means the offer depends on something. In this case it depends on pre-employment checks, such as identity, right to work, references and security clearance. When the checks are cleared, you are given a confirmed start date. Then you start the job. Some stages may be missing, and the order can change a little. The advert and the emails you receive will tell you what applies to your vacancy and give you dates for each stage.

items.title: L1: Sift, tests and interview explained
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: After you apply, your application is checked in the sift. Recruiters look for evidence that you meet each essential criterion. If you do not meet a criterion, you are normally sifted out. In some departments the sift is partly done by a computer system, but a person usually reviews the results. Some roles then ask you to take tests online. A verbal reasoning test checks how well you understand written information. A numerical reasoning test checks how well you work with numbers, tables and charts. A situational judgement test describes a work problem and asks how you would deal with it. Tests are often timed, so practice helps. If a test is part of the process, the department sends you a link and tells you how long you have to complete it. The interview comes next. Interviews for entry-level roles often ask about your past experience, such as a time you helped a customer, and about your strengths. Panel members are given a scoring guide. They score each answer against it. This keeps the process fair, because every candidate is scored in the same way. After the interview you are told the result. Feedback is often available if you ask.

items.title: L1: Offers and pre-employment checks
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: If an interview goes well, the department makes you an offer. It is a conditional offer, which means the job is yours only if you pass the pre-employment checks. These checks protect the public and the department. The first check is identity. You will be asked to show original documents such as a passport or driving licence. The second is right to work in the UK. The third is your employment history, often covering the last few years, and references from people who know your work. Many departments also carry out a criminal record check. The checks together are called the Baseline Personnel Security Standard, or BPSS. Some jobs need more security checking, called clearance. The levels include Counter Terrorist Check, Security Check and Developed Vetting. Entry-level office roles often need only the baseline checks, but the advert tells you. Checks take time, and some can take weeks. You will not get a start date until they are complete. Do not resign from your current job until you have the start date in writing. Be honest on every form. A false statement can lead to an offer being withdrawn. If you are unsure about something, ask the contact in your offer email.

items.title: L1: What fair recruitment means
items.body: Civil Service jobs are filled by fair and open competition and on merit. This is set out in the Recruitment Principles, which are published by the Civil Service Commission. The Commission is independent, which means it is separate from the government of the day. Merit means that the person who best meets the criteria for the job gets it. It does not matter who you know, what your background is, or whether you have friends in the department. Fair means that all candidates are treated in the same way. Open means that vacancies are advertised so that anyone eligible can apply. The aim is to select people on their ability to do the job. Departments should not treat people less favourably because of protected characteristics. These include age, disability, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation. This comes from the Equality Act 2010. Many departments also use name-blind sifting, where recruiters do not see names when screening. Candidates are assessed against the same criteria with the same methods. If you think a recruitment was not run fairly, you can complain to the department first. After that, the Civil Service Commission can look into a complaint about the Recruitment Principles.

items.title: L1: Disability Confident and the interview offer
items.source: Disability Confident scheme, GOV.UK; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Disability Confident is a government scheme that helps employers recruit and keep disabled people. The Civil Service takes part in the scheme. Employers can sign up at three levels: Disability Confident Committed, Disability Confident Employer and Disability Confident Leader. As part of the scheme, a disabled applicant who meets the minimum criteria for the role is offered an interview. The minimum criteria are the essential requirements listed in the advert. Meeting them does not guarantee a job, but it does guarantee the chance to be interviewed. This is sometimes called the guaranteed interview scheme. To use it, you tell the department on your application that you are disabled and want to be considered under the scheme. The definition of disability comes from the Equality Act 2010. It covers a physical or mental condition that has a substantial and long-term effect on your ability to do normal daily activities. Long-term usually means lasting, or likely to last, twelve months or more. The condition does not have to be visible. Examples include dyslexia, anxiety, diabetes and hearing loss. You do not have to tell an employer about a disability, but telling them lets them offer support. Information about your disability is treated in confidence.

items.title: L1: Reasonable adjustments
items.source: Equality Act 2010; Civil Service Jobs; Disability Confident guidance
items.body: A reasonable adjustment is a change that helps a person with a disability or health condition to take part fairly in recruitment or at work. The law requires employers to consider reasonable adjustments. This comes from the Equality Act 2010. Adjustments in recruitment might include extra time in a test, a different format such as large print, a more accessible interview room, a longer break between stages, or a BSL interpreter. At work, they might include a special keyboard, a quieter desk or flexible hours. You can ask for an adjustment at any stage. It is best to ask as early as you can, using the contact named in the advert. Describe what would help, for example extra time because of dyslexia. You do not need to use technical words. You may be asked for a little more information so the department can arrange the right support. Asking for an adjustment does not count against you. It does not change how your answers are scored. The scoring rules stay the same for everyone. The adjustment simply gives you a fair chance to show your ability. If the first adjustment does not work, tell the department and ask for a change.

items.title: L1: Working patterns and flexible working
items.source: Civil Service Jobs adverts; GOV.UK, Flexible working
items.body: The working pattern is the way your hours are arranged. It is shown on every Civil Service advert. Full time means working the full hours of the job. In the Civil Service this is often around 37 hours a week, although it can differ by department. Part time means working fewer hours. Job share means two people share one full-time job between them, each working part of the week. Flexible working means you have some choice over when you start and finish, within agreed limits. Hybrid working means a mix of time in the office and time working from home. Many Civil Service roles offer part-time, job-share and flexible working, which suits people with caring responsibilities, health needs or other commitments. Some jobs, such as those in public-facing offices, may need set hours or set days in the office. You can search by working pattern on Civil Service Jobs. If an advert does not say that a pattern is possible, you can ask the contact named in it. Employees in general have a legal right to ask for flexible working. The employer must consider the request fairly. Asking does not mean it will be agreed, but it should be considered in a reasonable way.

items.title: L1: Keeping track and meeting deadlines
items.body: Every Civil Service advert has a closing date and time. Applications that arrive late are not accepted. The website may be busy in the last hours before the deadline, and a connection or login problem on the final evening could cost you the application. Aim to submit well before the closing time, for example two or three days early. This also gives you time to read your answers again and fix mistakes. Keep a simple record of every role you apply for. A notebook, a spreadsheet or a note on your phone is enough. For each role write the reference number, the department, the job title, the closing date, what you submitted and the stage it has reached. Copy your application answers somewhere safe, because you can use them again for a similar role. Keep every email you get about interviews and tests. Check your messages regularly, because invitations may have a short reply time. Write down interview dates in a calendar, and set a reminder the day before. After an unsuccessful application, ask for feedback if it is offered, and use it to improve the next one. Many successful candidates apply for several roles before they get an offer, so keep going.
